How to ask a good question
  • Ask about one thing. A focused question gets a focused answer; “what about my life?” gets noise.
  • Give it a timeframe, like “over the next three months” or “by the end of the year”. Without one, the cards drift to whatever big event comes next.
  • Ask about the heart of the situation, not the side details.
  • For a yes or no, phrase it so it can be answered that way: “Will I … by …?”
  • If an answer worries you, don’t keep re-dealing until you like it. Narrow the question or change the timeframe instead.

You don’t have to type it. Keep the question clearly in mind while you shuffle, then choose good news or bad news below so the answer card is read the right way.

If the answer is yes, is that good news or bad news for you?

A yes to “Will I get the job?” is good news. A yes to “Will I lose my job?” is bad news. This decides how the answer card is read.

What the numbers and court cards mean

    About this reader

    How the shuffle works

    Each shuffle is a full Fisher–Yates shuffle driven by your browser’s cryptographic random number generator (crypto.getRandomValues), with rejection sampling so that no card is ever favoured. There’s no seed and no pattern. The deck keeps reshuffling until you tap Deal, then the cards come off the top, uncut, the way the book describes.

    Your questions and readings aren’t saved. They’re only sent to Claude when you ask for an AI reading, and the page remembers nothing but your last layout settings on this device.

    How the yes/no answer is decided

    One card gives the answer: position 6 in the Simple yes/no layout, position 10 in the Tree of Life, or the card itself in a single-card draw. As in the book, it’s read against your question. A favourable card means yes to something you hope for and no to something you fear; a difficult card means the opposite. A standstill card means nothing moves within your timeframe, so the answer is no for now, and the Wheel of Fortune means change is coming either way.

    Trumps carry the most weight. Gentle minor cards give a lean rather than a certainty. The other cards show how the answer comes about.

    How the AI reading works

    When you tap Get an AI reading, the page sends Claude your question, the layout, what each position means, and the cards that landed there with their meanings, along with the book’s reading rules. Claude explains these exact cards in their positions. It never draws new ones, and for yes/no readings it explains the verdict rather than changing it. Afterwards you can ask follow-up questions about the same cards.

    It runs on your own Claude account, and the first time you use it Claude asks for your permission. If Claude isn’t available where the page is open, the AI section doesn’t appear.

    Why there are no reversed cards

    The book doesn’t use reversals. Cards are always dealt upright, and some positions are marked as difficult instead. A card landing in one of those is read for its shadow: its gifts held back, or its trouble front and centre.

    Where the layouts and meanings come from

    The fourteen layouts and their diagrams follow Josephine McCarthy’s Tarot Skills for the 21st Century (TaDehent Books, 2020). Position descriptions are summarised here, and the card meanings are written for this reader in plain language. Where the book reads a card differently from most modern guides, this reader follows the book. For the full method and worked examples, read the book itself.

    The card images

    Scans of the original Rider–Waite–Smith deck, drawn by Pamela Colman Smith and first published in 1909. The artwork is in the public domain.

    Using readings wisely

    Readings are for reflection and guidance. They’re no substitute for medical, legal or financial advice, and a worrying card is a reason to look more closely, not to panic.
